summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with chronic systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and ongoing alcohol use, was admitted after a syncopal episode with a fall and head injury. He reported dizziness and a sensation of his implantable cardiac defibrillator firing, though device interrogation showed no recent activity. Initial evaluation revealed hypotension and lab findings consistent with dehydration, which improved with IV fluids. CT scans of the head and cervical spine showed no acute abnormalities, and a chest X-ray revealed a small right basilar opacity likely due to atelectasis. His symptoms were attributed to dehydration exacerbated by chronic alcohol use, Lasix therapy, and inappropriate use of nitroglycerin for device-pocket pain. His Lasix dose was adjusted to alternate between 20 mg and 40 mg daily, and he was counseled on hydration, avoiding alcohol, and not using nitroglycerin for non-cardiac pain. He was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up recommendations for primary care, liver monitoring, and device clinic evaluation for possible pocket revision.
